facts.text: Cordaitales, an order of gymnosperms, range from the Carboniferous into the Permian.

title: Kazakhstania collides with Siberia and Tarim

facts.text: Siberia, an independent continent since the early Paleozoic, collided with Kazakhstania, raising the Altai Mountains.
Closure of the Turkestan Ocean brought northern Tarim against Kazakhstania from the mid-Carboniferous to the start of the Permian.
With Kazakhstania joined to Laurussia, Siberia was effectively part of Pangaea by 310 Ma, though strike-slip motion went on into the Permian.

facts.text: The base of the Carboniferous is fixed at the La Serre section in Montagne Noire, southern France.
It is marked by the first appearance of the conodont Siphonodella sulcata, descended from S. praesulcata.
Later study found S. sulcata below the boundary, weakening the marker.

title: Crown tetrapods appear and take to land

facts.text: By the very start of the Carboniferous, stem tetrapods had split into two crown lines: one leading to modern amphibians, the other to amniotes.
The earliest confirmed land-dwelling tetrapods come from early Carboniferous deposits, some 20 million years after the first Devonian forms.
Lineages with extra digits died out, fixing hands and feet at no more than five digits.
Surviving tetrapods radiated on dry land and became the dominant land animals of the Carboniferous and Permian.

title: Romer's gap in the tetrapod record

facts.text: Tetrapod fossils are strikingly scarce from the Tournaisian into the early Visean, a span known as Romer's gap.
Land vertebrates were recovering from the Hangenberg extinction, and ichthyostegalian forms gave way to temnospondyls and reptiliomorphs.
Finds at Blue Beach, Nova Scotia, and in Scotland now show stem tetrapods and amphibians diversifying rapidly.

title: Tropical seas lay down the Carboniferous Limestone

facts.text: Warm, shallow tropical seas teeming with life laid down limestone widely across Britain and Ireland, in basins separated by landmasses such as the Wales-London-Brabant Massif.
The rock is built from the shells and hard parts of sea creatures such as corals, brachiopods and crinoids, set in carbonate mud.
Carbonates dominated the early Carboniferous across the British Isles and Western Europe; later uplifted, the limestone forms karst country such as the Mendips and Yorkshire Dales.

title: Crinoids at their peak

facts.text: Camerate crinoids peaked in diversity in the Mississippian; Agaricocrinus, about 345 Ma, was part of this echinoderm radiation.
Crinoids were so numerous that some Lower Carboniferous limestones near Clitheroe, England, consist almost entirely of their remains.
Their diversity fell from the Middle Mississippian as shell-crushing fish and sharks multiplied.

title: Sharks and ray-finned fish take over the seas

facts.text: After the end-Devonian Hangenberg extinction, sharks and their kin and ray-finned fish took over in diversity and abundance.
Few Devonian species of either group survived, so both had also suffered losses; no placoderm is confirmed in the Carboniferous.
Cartilaginous fish, especially holocephalans such as the stethacanthids, went through a major radiation.
Helicoprionids, eugeneodonts with a single circular tooth whorl in the lower jaw, first appeared.
The first large sharks, ratfishes and hagfish appear around 350 Ma.

title: Early Tournaisian Warm Interval

facts.text: After a brief glaciation at the Devonian–Carboniferous boundary, the climate warmed in the Early Tournaisian Warm Interval, 358–353 Ma.
Global average temperature was about 22 °C, with tropics near 30 °C and polar regions about 1.5 °C.

facts.text: By about 350 Ma, glacial strata were building up in sub-Andean basins of Bolivia, Argentina and Paraguay.
A mid-Tournaisian glaciation left species-poor frigid tundra in western Argentina.
These short, minor glaciations preceded the main ice age, part of a stepwise shift from greenhouse to icehouse.

title: First temnospondyls

facts.text: The earliest temnospondyl traces are Tournaisian footprints, about 350 Ma; the first body fossils, such as Balanerpeton, are Visean, around 330 Ma.
Temnospondyls, often seen as primitive amphibians, flourished worldwide through the Carboniferous, Permian and Triassic.
All their clades except the stereospondylomorphs, from edopoids to dissorophoids, appeared during the Carboniferous.
Their rise as dominant land vertebrates earned the Carboniferous the name 'Age of Amphibians'.

facts.text: Lepidodendron, a massive tree lycophyte, first appeared near the Tournaisian–Visean boundary.
Lepidodendron and Sigillaria went on to dominate the coal swamps, with horsetails and seed ferns between them.
Their order, the Lepidodendrales, ranges from the Carboniferous to the Late Permian.

Aragonite reef builders, including algae and sponges, appeared in the Pennsylvanian.

title: First winged insects

facts.text: The oldest known winged insects appear in the mid-Mississippian; flight may have evolved even earlier, in the Late Devonian.
Winged insects (pterygotes) went through a major radiation across the Carboniferous, 358 to 299 million years ago.
Sap-sucking palaeodictyopteroids dominated, and cockroach relatives (Blattoptera) became the most successful insects by the Pennsylvanian.
In the Pennsylvanian, Neoptera appeared and Miomoptera show the earliest evidence of complete metamorphosis.

facts.text: During the Visean Warm Interval glaciers nearly vanished, surviving only in the proto-Andes of Bolivia and Argentina and in highlands of Brazil and southwest Africa.

title: Carboniferous–Earliest Permian Biodiversification Event

facts.text: A long radiation of marine life, the Carboniferous–Earliest Permian Biodiversification Event, began in the Visean with the main phase of the ice age.
Fusulinid foraminifera and brachiopods led it; fusulinids diversified extremely fast, peaked in the Visean and later grew giant, some hosting photosynthetic algae.
Closure of the Rheic Ocean, falling sea level and Pangaea's assembly split the oceans into isolated regions, which may have driven it.
Bryozoans, renewed by the Hangenberg extinction, also peaked in the Visean, while cephalopods and swimming conodonts declined.

facts.text: The East Kirkton quarry in Scotland preserves land and freshwater animals; its richest layer dates to about 341 Ma, in the Visean.
It yielded dozens of early tetrapods, including the temnospondyl Balanerpeton and the proto-amniote Westlothiana ('Lizzie'), plus scorpions and eurypterids.
Its mostly land-dwelling fauna reflects a wider Carboniferous shift away from amphibious life.

title: Main phase of the Variscan (Hercynian) orogeny

facts.text: Gondwana and peri-Gondwanan terranes collided obliquely with Laurussia, with metamorphism, igneous activity and large-scale deformation; full collision came around 340 Ma.
Northwest Africa met southeastern Euramerica, raising the southern Appalachians and the Meseta and Mauritanide mountains.
Europe's Variscan orogeny and North America's Alleghanian orogeny were parts of one continental collision.
Its main (Sudetic) compressional phase ran from about 330 to 320 Ma, when Hercynian granites intruded central Europe.
Together with the Alleghanian, it raised the Central Pangean Mountains, complete by about 295 Ma at their greatest height.

title: Assembly of Pangaea

facts.text: Gondwana, Euramerica (Laurussia) and Siberia came together as the supercontinent Pangaea around 335 million years ago.
Plate motions sped up as Pangaea assembled, and the Rheic Ocean between Gondwana and Laurussia closed.
Blocks kept joining and rifting away into the early Mesozoic; Pangaea lasted about 160 million years, until its breakup began around 175 Ma.
Glacial deposits of this age, scattered from South America to Australia, later helped prove continental drift and the existence of Pangaea.

title: Main phase of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age

facts.text: The main phase of the ice age began between 335 and 330 Ma, in the late Visean, as the climate cooled and CO2 fell.
Its onset brought a global fall in sea level and unconformities lasting millions of years.
Ice spread from up to 30 centres across Gondwana; around 330 Ma an ice sheet kilometres thick covered much of Africa over the South Pole.
Glacial periods millions of years long alternated with warmer spells; the most intense phase came late in the Pennsylvanian.
Its glacial deposits reach 1,000 m thick in southern Africa's Dwyka Formation and 1,400 m in Brazil's Itararé Group.

facts.text: In the mid-Carboniferous, the South American part of Gondwana struck Laurussia's southern margin obliquely in the Ouachita orogeny, beginning in the Late Mississippian.
The uplifted Ouachita Mountains created foreland basins such as the Delaware Basin and fed rivers through the Pennsylvanian and Permian.

title: Serpukhovian extinction

facts.text: The largest extinction of the Carboniferous struck in the early Serpukhovian, removing about 31% of marine genera.
A major glaciation at the Visean–Serpukhovian boundary cooled the seas, and the extinction picked off species adapted to narrow, tropical temperature ranges.
Diverse Mississippian crinoid and rugose-coral communities gave way to species-poor, cosmopolitan ones; trilobites declined sharply while ammonoids peaked.
Driven more by low speciation than high extinction, its long-term ecological impact may have exceeded the end-Ordovician extinction's.
It ties with the Hangenberg event as the seventh-worst post-Cambrian mass extinction, though it may have been weaker in North America.

title: Deltas spread the Millstone Grit across northern England

facts.text: With Britain near the equator, rivers from northern uplands and the Wales-Brabant High carried sand and mud into the Pennine Basin.
When sea level fell as southern ice caps grew, deltas advanced across the region, leaving the thick sandstones of the Millstone Grit.
Lying beneath the Coal Measures, these gritstones now form the edges and moors of the Pennines and the Peak District.

title: First amniotes

facts.text: One tetrapod lineage evolved membranes around the embryo, so its eggs could survive on dry land: the amniotes.
Timelines place the first amniotes around 330 Ma, with Paleothyris among the earliest, 330–320 Ma; the Carboniferous article puts their first appearance in the late Carboniferous.
Clawed Tournaisian footprints from Australia's Snowy Plains Formation have been claimed as amniote tracks, which would push their origin to the start of the period or earlier.
Amphibians ruled until the mid-Carboniferous, when climate change cut their diversity and amniotes took over.

title: Alleghanian orogeny

facts.text: Africa, then part of Gondwana, collided with North America, part of Euramerica, in at least five deformation events.
The collision built the Appalachian and Allegheny Mountains, a wide, high chain along today's eastern seaboard.
It began about 325 Ma and lasted some 65 million years, into the Permian.
The collision helped form Pangaea; sediment from the rising mountains filled basins such as the Black Warrior Basin.
When West Africa struck in the Late Pennsylvanian, compression turned northwest and the same grinding raised the Little Atlas range around 300 Ma.

title: Mid-Carboniferous glacial maximum and sea-level fall

facts.text: The first major glacial period of the ice age, Serpukhovian to Moscovian, spread ice sheets from cores in southern Africa and South America.
In the Bashkirian a global fall in sea level marked the ice age's first major glacial maximum.
At the Mississippian–Pennsylvanian boundary, a positive oxygen-isotope excursion matched sea-level falls and widespread glacial deposits across southern Gondwana.
The low sea level left an unconformity that separates the Mississippian from the Pennsylvanian in North America.
Closure of the ocean gateway between the Rheic and Tethys in the early Bashkirian changed ocean circulation and added to the cooling.

title: Atmospheric oxygen peaks

facts.text: All models show oxygen rising from 15–20% at the start of the Carboniferous to highs of 25–30%, above today's 21%.
Pyrite records suggest about 15% early in the period, over 25% in the Pennsylvanian, then a drop below 20% toward its end.
Charcoal from wildfires grows more common from the Late Devonian into the Carboniferous, another sign of rising oxygen.
Coal-forest photosynthesis buried carbon as peat and released oxygen into the air.
How much the oxygen-rich air let arthropods and other life grow large is still debated.

title: CO2 falls to one of its all-time lows

facts.text: Atmospheric carbon dioxide crashed to one of its lowest levels ever in the Pennsylvanian and early Permian, falling below 300 ppm.
Burial of organic matter, widespread ocean anoxia and weathering of the rising Central Pangean Mountains drew it down, cooling the climate and triggering glaciation.
Fast-growing coal forests also locked away carbon; a very late Carboniferous forest resurgence cooled the globe and brought polar ice back to Gondwana.
Near the Carboniferous–Permian boundary, erosion of mafic mountain rocks pushed CO2 as low as 175 ppm, and it stayed under 400 ppm for 10 million years.
From a record low about 298 million years ago, CO2 rose fourfold by 294 million years ago.

facts.text: The Central Pangean Mountains set up a perennial monsoon over today's Europe and eastern North America, keeping them swampy while the Colorado Plateau stayed dry.
Climate models suggest the range helped lay down vast coal deposits.
The first signs of moisture moving toward the poles appeared in the late Carboniferous.

facts.text: Early rifting between India and the Cimmerian superterranes began in the Early Carboniferous.
The Cimmerian blocks rifted from Gondwana in the Late Carboniferous; they would dock with Asia in the Triassic and Jurassic.
Extension along Gondwana's northern margin late in the period set up the Cimmerian terrane's break-away and the opening of the Neo-Tethys in the early Permian.

title: Coal forests cover the tropics

facts.text: Vast freshwater swamp forests covered much of the tropical land in the late Carboniferous (Pennsylvanian), lasting into the Permian.
Towering lycopsid rainforests dominated equatorial Euramerica, the high point of Paleozoic land plants; peat mires also ringed the North and South China cratons.
Their buried peat became coal: about 90% of all coal beds formed in the Carboniferous and Permian, just 2% of Earth's history.
Why coal formation peaked is debated: a lag before lignin-digesting fungi evolved, or a unique mix of equatorial lands, high productivity and sinking wet basins.
Glacial sea-level falls exposed wide shelves where peat mires grew; rising interglacial seas then buried them.

title: Cyclothems record ice-age sea-level swings

facts.text: In the Pennsylvanian, repeating sediment cycles called cyclothems formed in shallow seas across tropical Laurussia and the China cratons.
Each records a sea-level fall and rise over about 100,000 years, as Gondwana's ice sheets advanced and retreated on a Milankovitch cycle.
The swings reached up to 120 m, with slow falls and rapid rises because ice sheets grow slowly but melt quickly.

title: Equatorial Pangaea dries out

facts.text: Pangaea's equatorial belt grew drier toward the end of the Carboniferous, beginning a dry trend that lasted into the Triassic.
Across the Carboniferous–Permian boundary, falling CO2 and low-latitude aridity brought a permanent shift to seasonally dry woodland.
Weaker continental weathering in the drier climate lowered the seawater strontium-isotope ratio toward the period's end.
After about 318 Ma, seasonality swung often between humid and arid; a cycle of aridification began in the late Moscovian, with abrupt faunal changes.
Late Pennsylvanian soils record drier, better-drained, more stable landscapes as the regional climate turned drier.

title: First conifers and cycads

facts.text: Cycads, the Callistophytales seed ferns and the Voltziales conifers appeared in the late Carboniferous; ginkgophytes also arose in the period.
Early walchian conifers such as Walchia favoured higher, drier ground, where gymnosperms grew in the Pennsylvanian.
The oldest probable cycad leaves, such as Crossozamia from South Korea and China, date to around 300 Ma.

title: Giant arthropods

facts.text: Arachnids, myriapods and especially flying insects underwent a major radiation in the late Carboniferous.
The millipede-like Arthropleura, up to 2.6 m long, was the largest land invertebrate of all time.
The griffinfly Meganeura, with a wingspan of about 75 cm, was the largest flying insect ever and dominated the skies around 305 Ma.
Giant insects, millipedes and scorpions thrived while tetrapods stayed small, until the rainforest collapse.
The gigantism may reflect high oxygen levels, though how oxygen shaped body size is debated.

title: Oslo Rift begins to form

facts.text: Around today's Oslo, the main phase of graben formation began in the late Carboniferous, as tectonic forces tore the crust apart in the last phase of the Variscan orogeny.
Rifting coincided with the Moscovian–Kasimovian boundary and the Carboniferous rainforest collapse.
It culminated in heavy volcanism; in Vestfold, rhomb porphyry lavas piled up about 3,000 m thick.

title: Uralian orogeny begins

facts.text: The Uralian orogeny, which raised the Ural Mountains, began in the Late Carboniferous, about 323 Ma, and went on through the Permian.
Kazakhstania began colliding with Laurussia as the Ural Ocean closed in the Bashkirian.
Siberia, Kazakhstania and Baltica collided to form Laurasia, the basis of most of present-day Eurasia.
Deformation continued into the Permian, with granites intruding the region; around 300 Ma the Urals were uplifted as Pangaea was finally sutured.
The Magnitogorsk island arc in the Ural Ocean collided with Baltica's passive margin from the Late Devonian to early Carboniferous.

title: Synapsids and sauropsids split

facts.text: Amniotes split into two lines: synapsids, the mammal lineage, and sauropsids, the line of reptiles and birds.
Timelines place the first sauropsids around 320 Ma and the first synapsids around 318 Ma; the earliest fossils of both date to about 313 Ma.
Synapsid pelycosaurs appeared in the Late Carboniferous and went on to dominate land for some 40 million years.
By the end of the period amniotes had diversified into pelycosaur families, protorothyridids, captorhinids, saurians and araeoscelids.

title: Karoo Basin begins filling with glacial deposits

facts.text: Subduction under Gondwana and the rising Gondwanide mountains made room for a foreland basin, the Karoo Basin, across southern Africa.
Southern Africa lay within the Antarctic Circle; ice sheets buried the highlands around the young basin, while floating glaciers filled its lowlands.
Their tillites, diamictites and striated pavements, the Dwyka Group, begin the Karoo Supergroup and reach about 800 m thick in the south.

facts.text: The Joggins Fossil Cliffs of Nova Scotia preserve a diverse land ecosystem of lycopsids, giant arthropods and fish.
Joggins yields Hylonomus, the oldest known sauropsid and one of the oldest reptiles in the fossil record.

title: Kiaman Reverse Superchron begins

facts.text: Earth's magnetic field held reversed polarity, without flipping, for more than 50 million years, from about 312 to 262 Ma.
The Kiaman superchron spans the late Carboniferous to the late Permian; comparable spells are the Cretaceous Normal Superchron and a possible Ordovician one.

title: Mazon Creek fossil beds

facts.text: Near Morris, Illinois, a large delta preserved fossils in ironstone concretions in exceptional detail, including the enigmatic Tullimonstrum, known only from here.
Its roughly 200 insect species, some gigantic, show insects already filled their main modern niches as herbivores, detritivores and insectivores.

title: Brief, intense Kasimovian glaciation

facts.text: Early in the Kasimovian a short (<1 million years) but intense glaciation drove CO2 as low as 180 ppm.
It ended abruptly as CO2 rose quickly, after wetland forests had been restructured and tree lycopsids lost.

facts.text: A relatively warm interglacial spanning the Kasimovian and Gzhelian, the Alykaevo Climatic Optimum, separated the ice age's first and second major glacial periods.

title: Carboniferous rainforest collapse

facts.text: A cooler, drier climate fragmented and then collapsed the coal-forest rainforests; tree lycopsids and other wetland groups were lost in the Kasimovian glacial interval.
Lycopsid forests gave way to tree-fern forests: a complex replacement, not the loss of all rainforest.
Scale trees largely vanished from North America and Europe but persisted in Cathaysia, where coal forests revived at the very end of the period.
Amphibians and amniotes were both hit; the collapse may have let amniotes overtake amphibians, and seed plants overtake ferns and lycophytes.
A minor marine and land extinction, it left vast deserts across the continental interior.

facts.text: Around 300 Ma, in the Pennsylvanian, mountain building raised the Ancestral Rocky Mountains in what are now Colorado and New Mexico, with a prong into Wyoming.
The Colorado orogeny that built them also began the Denver Basin; the range later eroded away.

title: Ice age peaks at the end of the Carboniferous

facts.text: An exceptionally intense cooling struck around 300 Ma, when a very large part of Gondwana lay under glacial conditions.
A second major glacial period began in the late Gzhelian, with ice sheets spreading from cores in Australia and India into the early Permian.
The ice age peaked across the Carboniferous–Permian boundary; in the glacial maximum, 299–293 Ma, global average temperature was about 13 °C.
Brazil's Paraná Basin had its last glaciation in the early Gzhelian.
